name: Sadar Bazaar (Main Bazaar Street)
why: Pushkar's central shopping street; Wikivoyage calls the town overall 'the best place to shop in Northern India', with jewellery, clothing, cushion covers, decorative items, books, bags, handicrafts and footwear lining this street. The same source warns prices are cheap but quality is often subpar.
warn: Exact shutter-up/shutter-down times for the bazaar itself could not be independently confirmed via a live source this session. Two central Pushkar cafes (not shops) keep hours of roughly 09:00/09:30 to 22:30/23:00, which gives a rough proxy for how late the town centre stays active, but that is circumstantial, not bazaar-shop data - do not treat it as confirmed shop hours.

name: Sarafa Bazaar
why: 'Sarafa' means goldsmith/moneychanger in most North Indian bazaars, so the name marks this as Pushkar's traditional jewellers' street. A travel guide lists it as a popular market for 'traditional handicrafts at affordable rates', which is the closest live description found this session.
warn: No independent second source cross-checked this session; treat the exact boundary of this market as approximate.

name: Bada Bazaar
why: Listed by a travel guide as one of Pushkar's traditional in-town markets (source spells it 'Baza Bazar', almost certainly a rendering of Bada Bazar, 'big market').
warn: Spelling and exact extent not cross-checked against a second source this session.

name: Kedalganj Bazaar
why: Named market area named in the brief for this research. No live source could be located this session confirming its exact location, goods mix, or standing inside Pushkar's bazaar layout.
warn: Unverified this session - do not treat anything about this entry (existence, location, contents) as confirmed until checked on the ground or against a source.

name: Halwai Gali
why: 'Halwai' means confectioner/sweet-maker in Hindi, so a 'Halwai Gali' would by naming convention be a sweet-makers' lane - a pattern that recurs in many North Indian old-city bazaars (e.g. one exists near the Dargah in nearby Ajmer). No live source could confirm this specific stretch exists by that name inside Pushkar this session.
warn: Unverified this session - treat as a naming hypothesis, not a confirmed location, until checked on the ground.

name: Brahma Temple approach-lane market
why: The shop-lined approach to the Brahma Temple is called out by a travel guide as offering 'a wide variety of handicrafts'. The temple is Pushkar's single biggest footfall draw, which makes this lane the most tourist-dense shopping stretch in town.
warn: Expect the highest opening-quote inflation in town here precisely because footfall is highest and dwell time is short (people are walking to/from the temple, not browsing at leisure).

name: Silver jewellery shops
why: Wikivoyage explicitly lists jewellery among Pushkar's main shopping categories; a second guide specifically calls out 'silver oxidised jewellery' lining the main street.
warn: See buy.json for how to check for a genuine BIS hallmark before paying silver prices for plated base metal.

name: Gemstone and semi-precious stone stalls
why: Loose and set semi-precious stones are commonly sold alongside silver jewellery in Indian pilgrim/backpacker bazaars generally. Could not find a Pushkar-specific source distinguishing this cluster from the general jewellery trade this session.
warn: A large share of stalls' 'gemstones' in tourist markets nationwide are dyed glass or plastic; see buy.json for the bubble/hardness checks.

name: Mojari / jutti shoe shops
why: Mojari are a Rajasthan-wide leather-footwear craft; Wikivoyage lists footwear among the categories of goods sold in Pushkar's shops.
warn: Traditional lasts run narrow/flat with no left-right distinction on cheaper pairs - try them on rather than trusting a quoted size.

name: Leather bag shops
why: Leather goods, including bags, are explicitly listed by Wikivoyage among what Pushkar's shops sell.
warn: Check stitching at handle-join stress points before buying; bazaar-grade bags typically fail there first, not at the leather panel itself.

name: Mirror-work and embroidery textile shops
why: A travel guide specifically calls out 'miniature paintings, mirror work, and hand embroidery' among Pushkar's handicrafts.
warn: Glued-on mirrors (a shortcut on cheaper pieces) pop out with normal wear; hand-stitched mirrors are set into a buttonhole-stitch frame.

name: Block print fabric shops
why: Block-printed fabric is sold widely in Pushkar's bazaars as part of the general Rajasthani textile trade. The historic hand block-print production centres are Sanganer and Bagru near Jaipur, not Pushkar - what is sold locally is largely brought in rather than printed on site. This regional-craft context was not independently re-verified via a live source this session.
warn: Assume stock was made elsewhere and shipped in unless a specific seller can demonstrate otherwise.

name: Bedcover and tapestry shops
why: Bedcovers and tapestry-style wall hangings fall under the 'cushion covers ... decorative items' that Wikivoyage explicitly lists as sold in Pushkar's shops.
warn: A hand-finished hem is slightly uneven; a machine-overlocked hem is perfectly uniform - useful quick check for how the piece was actually made.

name: Rose product shops (gulkand, rose water, rose oil)
why: Wikipedia describes Pushkar as 'the rose garden of Rajasthan' because of commercial rose cultivation whose essence is exported internationally - the direct reason gulkand, rose water and rose oil are sold as local specialties here rather than as generic imported goods.
warn: No verified price anchor found this session for any rose product; see buy.json for physical checks (petal texture in gulkand, scent/residue tests for rose water and oil).

name: Incense and attar shops
why: Standard offering-economy stalls around a major temple town; Pushkar's Brahma Temple and ghats draw heavy pilgrim footfall which sustains dedicated incense/attar stalls in the bazaar. Not a claim of local manufacture - India's historic attar-distillation centre is Kannauj, Uttar Pradesh, not Pushkar.
warn: 'Pure attar' claims are effectively unverifiable by eye at the stall; see buy.json for the oil-vs-alcohol paper test.

name: Brass and metalwork shops
why: Brass devotional items (lamps, idols, bells) are standard stock in Indian temple-town bazaars. This is inferred under Wikivoyage's general 'decorative items/handicrafts' listing rather than a category named specifically for Pushkar by a source this session.
warn: Category not independently confirmed as a distinct Pushkar specialty this session; no price anchor sourced.

name: Musical instrument stalls
why: Small Rajasthani folk-instrument stalls (khartal, ravanahatha, ektara) are a common feature of pilgrim/backpacker bazaars across Rajasthan. Could not confirm this as a named Pushkar specialty via a live source this session.
warn: Many tourist-stall instruments are display pieces only and cannot actually be played in tune; test before buying if playability matters to you.

name: Hippie / festival clothing stalls
why: Pushkar has a long-documented backpacker/'hippie trail' presence tied to its Camel Fair, which Wikivoyage says draws roughly 400,000 visitors a year; loose festival-style clothing stalls catering to this crowd are a well-known feature of the town's bazaars.
warn: Loose-weave cotton/rayon prints can run colour badly in the wash; ask to feel/wash-test a corner before buying.

name: Camel leather goods stalls
why: Pushkar hosts one of India's largest camel fairs - Wikivoyage cites over 11,000 camels, horses and cattle traded there annually - which is the direct link to camel-leather goods (bags, mojari trim, belts) being sold locally.
warn: 'Camel leather' claims are effectively unverifiable by a buyer on the spot; cow leather is frequently sold under the camel-leather label.

name: Bandhani / tie-dye shops
why: Bandhani tie-dye is a Rajasthan/Gujarat-wide craft (Wikipedia); it is sold widely in Pushkar's bazaars as part of the general regional textile trade rather than being produced specifically in Pushkar itself.
warn: See buy.json for the hand-knot vs machine-print test.

name: Secondhand book exchange stalls
why: Pushkar's long-stay backpacker/hippie-trail culture, tied to the Camel Fair crowd Wikivoyage describes, commonly sustains secondhand-book exchange stalls in similar Indian backpacker towns. No specific named Pushkar shop could be confirmed via a live source this session.
warn: Category itself is unverified for Pushkar specifically this session - included as a plausible feature of the backpacker bazaar, not a confirmed one.

name: Spice and pickle stalls
why: A travel guide lists 'food items like pickles and masalas' among what's sold in Pushkar's markets.
warn: Buy whole spices where possible - they're much harder to adulterate than pre-ground ones.

name: Honey stalls
why: Local/wild honey is commonly sold in Rajasthani pilgrim-town bazaars generally. Could not confirm this as a named Pushkar specialty via a live source this session; included per the requested coverage but flagged as unverified for Pushkar.
warn: Category unverified for Pushkar specifically this session; no price anchor sourced.

name: General handicraft stalls
why: Wikivoyage groups much of Pushkar's general retail simply as 'handicrafts', alongside jewellery, clothing, cushion covers, decorative items, books, bags and footwear, and adds that a rural-market fringe on the outskirts carries rarer traditional crafts.
warn: The same source's one hard quality warning applies here too: prices are cheap, but quality is often subpar.
